results.content: Building a startup for a target market is not a logical exercise. It's an emotional one. Your customers' wants and needs sound good on paper when you are first doing discovery. But... Three months later, you show up at their door with a sock full of pennies asking why they haven’t signed up…you realize NEEDing something is different than BUYING it. I think a good startup needs three things... 1. A Good Problem/Pain. 2. A Good Pitch (this is usually the emotional part) and 3. A Good Product. You can get by with 2 of these for a little while, but the third will always come back to haunt you. Look at Notion for example. I bet you 95% of their customer base has Microsoft Office or Google Docs... so there is no immediate pain or problem they were actually solving. Yet their product was sexy [...] that finally worked. Every mistake shaped the system that now runs smoother, scales faster, and actually helps people. ✅ Consistency beats creativity when it comes to growth ✅ Feedback is not criticism, it’s free consulting ✅ Great products are not built once, they evolve every single day I’ve realized that ideas are easy to fall in love with, but execution is where they’re tested. You can have the smartest blueprint, but if you’re not ready to rebuild it from scratch, it won’t survive the real world. What separates successful founders from dreamers isn’t luck, it’s patience. The ability to take a broken version, learn from it, and come back stronger.
